To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a scorpion toxin, maurocalcine, binds to ryanodine receptors and alters the process of calcium channel closure, leading to uncontrolled calcium release in the absence of membrane depolarization.

the scorpion toxin peptide maurocalcine, which is a potent activator of the skeletal muscle ryanodine calcium release channel, induces a transient loss of voltage control over calcium release when applied to intact muscle fibers.

a scorpion toxin, MCa, injected into skeletal muscle fibers induces a prolonged phase of Ca2+ elevation following membrane repolarizations, with no concurrent membrane current, and that the magnitude of this uncontrolled extra phase is proportional to the peak Ca2+ release during membrane depolarizations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a transient, but significant, alteration of voltage control of SR calcium release in the presence MCa in skeletal muscle.
the molecular basis of voltage sensing by the ryanodinereceptor.
the molecular mechanisms of Ca(2+)-release channel regulation by the voltage-sensing DHPr and the role of the cytoplasmic loops of the channel in the process of Ca(2) + release.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MCa is a specific inhibitor of the repolarization-dependent inactivation of the RYr.
MCa, in the presence of depolarization, causes a transient loss of voltage control in skeletal muscle.
the MCa binding to RYr is responsible for a transient loss of voltage control on calcium release.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MCa, a toxin that binds to RYrs, alters the process of calcium release termination in skeletal muscle.
the voltage dependence of the RYr channel can be modified by MCa in a way that leads to a transient loss of control by the DHPr.
in the presence of MCa, the SR release channel is no more sensitive to the membrane voltage.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in contrast with the previous reports, MCa does not alter the voltage dependence of SR calcium release in skeletal muscle, and the effect of MCa is limited to an uncontrolled phase of Ca((2+)) release that occurs after the membrane repolarization.
the MCa-induced uncontrolled calcium release in skeletal muscle fibers can be explained by a transient loss of voltage control.
MCa, by interacting with the RYr, induces a long-lasting phase of uncontrolled Ca(2+) leak, thus leading to an unphysiologically large Ca(2+) increase in skeletal muscle.
